title: Cosmetics throw on bots, and the hat is silently lost
description:
Not reported by anybody. Found in Cowser's debug bundle while triaging the
seven-player report, in `sourcemod/errors_20260824.log`.

    [SM] Exception reported: Assertion failed - wearable entity 589 not attached
         to player. Gamedata may need to be updated
    [SM] Blaming: tf2utils.smx
    [SM]   [3] TF2Util_EquipPlayerWearable
    [SM]   [4] Line 221, .../redbots3/cosmetics.sp::WearHat
    [SM]   [5] Line 129, .../redbots3/cosmetics.sp::Timer_GiveBotCosmetics

Three times across two maps (rottenburg and coaltown), each on a different
wearable entity, so it is not one bad item id.

Low priority on its own: the throw is caught by SourceMod, the bot plays fine,
and only the hat is lost. It is filed because an unhandled exception in a timer
is the kind of thing that stops being cosmetic later, and because the log line
suggests the real cause is elsewhere.

## Worth checking

The tf2utils assertion says the wearable is not attached to the player at the
moment we equip it. Two readings, and they want different fixes:

- We are equipping too early, before the bot's wearable is attached. Then the
  fix is ours: check attachment before calling, or move the work later in
  `Timer_GiveBotCosmetics`.
- tf2utils' own gamedata is stale, which is what the message literally suggests.
  Then the fix is a version bump, and we should confirm the pinned tf2utils is
  current before writing any code.

Check the second one first, since it is a version lookup rather than a debug
session.

Separately, `WearHat` should handle the failure rather than let it throw. The
same log shows the hat pool already dropping items it knows a class cannot wear
("Item 30928 cannot be worn by class 1 and has been dropped from the hat pool"),
so the surrounding code already has a way to say no. This path should use it.

title: Native Linux servers crash far more than Docker or Windows
description:
Reported from play: a native Linux server crashes far more often than the same
mod under Docker or on Windows. Not measured here, and the test-bed is Linux
inside Docker, so this is the one platform nothing in this repo exercises.

What is known, in order of how much evidence there is.

**A file replaced under a running server is fatal on Linux and refused on
Windows.** This repo has already been bitten by it once: `testbed/entrypoint.sh`
copied the staged tree over the running server every thirty seconds with `cp -r`,
and `cp` truncates before it writes. A loaded extension is mmap'd, truncating the
file invalidates the pages under it, and the next instruction out of that
extension is a SIGBUS. Five or six crashes in ten minutes, with the backtrace
naming whichever extension the loop had just rewritten. Windows refuses to
overwrite a file a running process has mapped, so the same deploy silently does
nothing instead of corrupting the server, and a Wine run that happened to have no
supervising loop read as a platform difference for a day. `cp -ru`, or stop the
server before copying.

**So the first question is whether the native deploy writes into a live server
directory** while it runs: an update script, a sync, an editor saving into
`tf/addons`. That is the shape that produces "Linux crashes more" with no code
difference at all.

**Memory pressure.** The watchdog measures frame time, and a page fault that
stalls a frame is indistinguishable from an infinite loop. A session went from
six clean waves to four failed runs in a row with 200 MB free and swap-in at
20 MB/s, code unchanged. `run.sh` refuses to start below 1500 MB now for exactly
this reason.

**Docker hides crashes.** The container restarts srcds by itself, so a crash
there reads as a hiccup while the same crash natively ends the session. Some of
the difference may be reporting rather than rate.

To settle it rather than guess, get a symbolised backtrace. Enable core dumps,
then copy `bin/`, `tf/bin/` and `tf/addons/sourcemod/{bin,extensions}` out of the
server and point gdb at them:

    gdb -batch -ex 'set sysroot /tmp/tfdbg' \
        -ex 'set solib-search-path /tmp/tfdbg/bin:/tmp/tfdbg/tf/bin:...' \
        -ex 'bt 25' /tmp/tfdbg/srcds_linux core.NNN

An unsymbolised trace is what kept the last one open for two sessions; with the
libraries in place it named the frame in one go.
notes:
Deprioritised, P1 to P3, and worked around rather than solved.

The launcher now passes -nowatchdog on Linux and only on Linux
(srcdsArgs in launcher/internal/runtime/runtime.go, where -nocrashdialog
already splits the two platforms; test TestTheWatchdogIsOffOnLinuxOnly).

The evidence is from the stress session that took the desktop down with it. The
watchdog build died inside nine minutes at load 7-8. The same load against
-nowatchdog held rcon on all twelve probes with no restart. That matches the
shape of the report: Docker and Windows are not affected, and the watchdog is
what kills a Linux server on a slow frame that neither of the others treats as
fatal.

What is given up is the kill on a genuinely hung frame, so a real infinite loop
now hangs where it used to restart. That is the better failure. It leaves a live
process to attach to instead of a core, and every hang this mod has actually
produced was a slow frame rather than a hang: mvm-297 was an unbounded nav mesh
search that tripped the watchdog and was fixed with PATHS_PER_FRAME.

Left at P3 rather than closed because the underlying question is untouched: why
a native Linux server takes frames long enough to trip a watchdog that Docker on
the same kernel does not. Nothing here answers that. If the crash reports stop,
this can close as won; if they keep coming with no watchdog in the picture, the
cause was never the watchdog and this bead is where that gets picked up.

Docker is deliberately not changed. It is not the platform being reported, its
arguments come from the upstream image's entry.sh rather than from us, and
changing an unaffected platform would remove the comparison this bead rests on.

testbed/run-native.sh takes TESTBED_SRCDS_EXTRA so a run can be pointed either
way without editing the script, which is how the two builds were compared.

comments.author: m-this
comments.text:
There is a native bed now, mvm 7beba7e:

    testbed/seed-native.sh                 once, copies the game out of the container
    testbed/run-native.sh --waves 12       same flags as run.sh
    testbed/symbolise-core.sh core.1234    a backtrace with names in it

It runs srcds_linux directly rather than through srcds_run, so a crash stays
crashed and leaves a core instead of being restarted underneath the measurement,
which is the thing the container bed cannot show. It writes the same server.cfg
as the container by sourcing entrypoint.sh, so the two beds differ in the one
variable this is about.

Three things it cost, all worth knowing for anyone standing one up:

- The exclude when copying the game has to be anchored. An unanchored core.*
  also matches SourceMod's core.games.txt and core.phrases.txt; the server then
  starts, fails to parse its gamedata and never answers rcon.
- srcds takes the console over after the Steam banner and writes nothing more to
  a redirected stdout. That reads exactly like a server that never started.
  Readiness is asked of rcon.
- The host needs a 32 bit C++ runtime. Rather than a package, seed-native.sh puts
  the image's own into the game's bin/, which srcds_run already has on its
  library path.

Running a native sample now. Whatever it says, the recipe is the useful half:
the same three commands on the machine that actually crashes will produce a
symbolised backtrace, and that is what this issue is short of.

comments.author: m-this
comments.text:
Measured with the whole player stack, and it does not reproduce here.

The native bed now loads tf2-archipelago's plugin beside the bots
(TESTBED_ARCHIPELAGO_SMX) and the bridge runs in test mode, so the integration is
genuinely live: the fake room recorded checks and death-link traffic while the
run played. Native srcds, the bots mod, the archipelago plugin and a bridge, on
Debian 13, alone on the machine:

                          waves  worst frame in a wave  slow  stalled  worst before a wave
  native, bots only         12          87 ms            274     0          146 ms
  native + archipelago       7          82 ms            245     0          109 ms

No crash, no stalled frame, and the wave start is if anything quieter with the
plugin than without. So on this machine the integration does not trip the
watchdog, and the plugin's own mvm_begin_wave handler is three integer
assignments and one timer, with its debug logging compiled to an early return
when the convar is off.

What is still different from a player's server, in the order I would test them:

- The launcher runs srcds through srcds_run, this bed runs srcds_linux directly.
  srcds_run adds the restart loop and the steamclient dlopen.
- Humans connected. Every measurement here has an idle fake client and no real
  ones, and joining, choosing a class and the bot kicked to make room for them
  are all wave-start work this never does.
- Their hardware and what else it is doing. A page fault that stalls a frame is
  an infinite loop as far as the watchdog is concerned.

The decisive run is on the machine that crashes:

    TESTBED_NATIVE_ROOT=~/path/to/tf2ap/tf-dedicated testbed/run-native.sh --waves 12

and if it dies, testbed/symbolise-core.sh on the core it leaves. That gives a
named frame instead of 'it crashed', which is what this issue is short of.

comments.author: m-this
comments.text:
Numbers for it, from 30 waves of test-bed runs on the current build. The stats plugin has been measuring frame times all along and nothing had read them for this.

  mean frame                                   15.0 ms, which is the tick
  worst frame inside a wave                    median 113 ms, max 172 ms
  frames over the slow mark, per wave          median 18, max 43
  frames stalled, per wave                     median 1, max 8
  worst frame in the break before a wave       median 121 ms, MAX 1796 ms

The last line is where the stutter lives. Inside a wave the worst frame is about
seven ticks; in the break before one it reaches 1796 ms, which is more than a
second of the server not moving, and it lands right where a player is watching
the wave bar. Twelve hundred of that was once traced to the map still loading,
so the number wants splitting by how long the map has been up before it is
trusted; docs/testbed-metrics.md has that warning.

Worth knowing about the two known causes, both now fixed, because a rerun should
show whether anything is left: an unbounded nav mesh search killed frames badly
enough to trip the watchdog (mvm-297, fixed with PATHS_PER_FRAME), and
IsPathToVectorPossible reads like a cheap predicate and is a full NavAreaBuildPath.

The 'stall' event the plugin writes did not fire once across those 30 waves, so
whatever FRAME_STALL_MS is set to is above what these runs produce; a report of
a visible stutter at 113 ms means the threshold, not the server, is what needs
changing before this can be measured from a results file.
